1|# COUPLE BIBLE — CANON (Day 1)
2|
3|## WHO THEY ARE
4|
5|**Elias Ward**, 35. Runs "Ward & Son," a two-van heating-and-plumbing crew. There is no son and never was — his father Tom started the company; Tom died three years ago and Elias kept the name because repainting both vans felt like losing him twice. Left school at 17 to work under his dad. Hands always smell faintly of flux and solder. Married 4 years (anniversary: 12 September), together 8. Lives in a 1930s semi on Ferndale Road.
6|
7|**Maren Ward**, 33 (née Kowalczyk — she kept her name professionally; his mother "forgets" it constantly). Charge nurse, paediatric ward at St Aldhelm's, rotating day/night shifts. Daughter of Polish immigrants; grew up translating hospital letters for her mother. Organised to the point of ritual: labelled jars, a shared calendar nobody else maintains, a notebook of "things Elias almost said."
8|
9|## QUIRKS
10|
11|- Elias: fixes things around the house *instead of* talking — she'll wake to a silenced door hinge mid-argument. Writes reminders on the back of his hand. Calls her "Mare" and nothing else.
12|- Maren: narrates traffic when driving ("indicator, love, it's free"). Sings specific songs badly when anxious — ABBA's "Slipping Through My Fingers," always that one. Keeps the notebook; page one is dated their wedding day.
13|
14|## THE THING EACH NEVER SAYS ALOUD
15|
16|- **Elias:** that he's terrified he'll be bad at marriage the way his dad was bad at it — Tom provided brilliantly and vanished emotionally — and that every silent fixed hinge is him begging without having to.
17|- **Maren:** that she's started keeping score — that his family takes and hers thanks — and that she's frightened the marriage is becoming logistics: two calendars negotiating custody of a weekend.
18|
19|## THE THREE LIVE TENSIONS
20|
21|1. **MONEY — the £9,400.** Six weeks ago Elias moved £9,400 out of the joint "Ferndale Fund" (house-deposit savings, 3 years of skimming) to cover his brother Callum's defaulted van-lease. Told her nothing. She found it on a paper statement Tuesday. His position: it's my brother, it's my money too, problem solved. Hers: the amount is survivable; the secrecy is not. Last night ended: her — "I'm not angry about the money." Him — "Then what?" Neither answered. She slept facing the wall.
22|
23|2. **FAMILY — two mothers, one compass.** Maren's mother **Beata** (61, early Parkinson's, 90 minutes away in Leeds) asked gently last week whether they'd ever consider moving closer — Maren wants to say yes and hasn't dared. Elias's mother **Pat** (66, ten minutes away, Sunday roast is law) treats Maren's nursing as "a phase she'll grow out of" and the surname as a personal insult. Each spouse privately believes the other's family always wins.
24|
25|3. **TIME — four dinners.** His crew takes emergency call-outs nights and weekends; she rotates shifts. Maren counted: four dinners together last month, one without phones. The shared calendar she built has become a battlefield — he double-books it, then apologises with flowers, which she has started putting in the boot-room vase without comment.
26|
27|## STATE GOING INTO DAY 1
28|
29|It's Thursday. Tonight's 7pm dinner at Trattoria Verde — booked two weeks ago, the "proper talk" Maren demanded — collides with a £400 emergency boiler call-out Elias took at 4:40pm because the Ferndale Fund hole suddenly makes money real. Pat has invited herself and Callum to Sunday roast. Beata's specialist appointment landed Tuesday 10:40 in Leeds and needs a driver. Everything above is canon; nothing else has happened yet.

1|# BOY_IN — Day 5 (for Elias)
2|
3|## WHERE YOU ARE
4|Monday, 7:05am, kitchen, Ferndale Road. The frost is a memory — grey drizzle, and the board is back to earth: three callbacks from the weekend surge, a landlord warranty job, nothing heroic. Half a frost morning still paid like a full week of radiators, and today the first £150 leaves the account under the only terms the Ferndale Fund has ever had with both names on them. Yesterday you walked into your mum's at ten past one, together; at two you sat in Tom's chair and said things at that table nobody's said in twenty years. At 8:05 Callum: "sound yesterday that. good do. cheers mate" — friendly as a labrador, and not one word about money. At 8:20 your mother: "Lovely yesterday. Four of us round one table — your dad would've called that a win." Today is the deadline you set out loud over gravy: a number or a no.
5|
6|## WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE TODAY
7|- Sunday you merged the collision instead of winning it: worked till noon, quit it, rode shotgun at 12:44 — "together or not at all," her words returned as your rule. The table stayed one table; Pat's split died before the puds.
8|- At two you sat in Dad's chair and said the missing-him part out loud. Her hand landed where you'd asked it to. The deeper sentence — terrified of being Tom — still hasn't been said in those words.
9|- Callum: boxed at one o'clock, beers after pudding, the £200 unmentioned, buried till Monday by your own ruling. He brought beers and zero mention of £200. Today the grave opens, and you're the one holding the shovel.
10|- The fund: £150 a month, review on demand — your scale, her pick, signed. It fires today.
11|
12|## TODAY'S PRESSURES
13|1. Deadline day, and the lad's just been nice. "Number or a no" was easy to say at a Sunday table; it's harder to text a brother who opens with cheers mate. Ask-first was never just for her — it's the family trade now, and Callum's the next patient.
14|2. The £150 fires today — first jointly-signed debit in the fund's history. One small line on a statement; the biggest structural change since the hole.
15|3. Pat's text quotes the ghost approvingly — Dad would've called it a win — the morning after you sat in his chair. Grief has a hangover. You know the drill: say the thing or it says you.
16|4. Tomorrow, 10:40, Mare's in Leeds with her mum at the specialist. Anything unsaid tonight waits a day and shares her with a ward.
17|
18|## REMINDER (your own words, keep them close)
19|Dad provided brilliantly and vanished emotionally, and you learned both halves before you were seventeen — but Sunday you asked for an arm-touch instead of toughing it, and it landed. Same trade today, different brother: a number or a no, said like a request, not a warrant.

2|
3|## WHERE YOU ARE
4|Monday, 7:40am, St Aldhelm's staff room. Day shift, home by six if the ward behaves. Yesterday: windscreen scraped at 12:40, passenger seat occupied at 12:44, one table, his hand flat where your arm could reach it — and the sentence about his dad said out loud at that table for the first time in twenty years. You paid him for 12:44 in the car — "I notice everything you do on purpose lately" — and the blue coat is on the door for tomorrow. At 8:10 your mum: "All set for tomorrow, love. 10:40, Dr Okafor. The letter says he'll talk options — you'll listen properly, you always remember it better than me. No rush if the roads are bad. X." And the rota flags it before you've finished your coffee: tomorrow's evening clinic has doubled, they'll ring this morning.
5|

7|- Saturday you picked the number — £150, review on demand — and today it fires: the first jointly-set debit the Ferndale Fund has ever had. Watch what it feels like: partnership or paperwork.
8|- Sunday the doctrine met the driveway and won without a fight. The loaded line landed once over the gravy and didn't need a second swing. Callum performed; the £200 stayed buried, till Monday — his deadline, his shovel.
9|- The longer sentence — "trying looks like asking now" — rides in your throat, staged for tomorrow's car, where nobody reports back.
10|- Pat's reform: one clean Sunday. Durability unknown.
11|

13|1. The rota rings this morning: Tuesday evening clinic, runs late, can you do it — the fallback you offered in a moment of wanting to be needed. It collides head-on with the drive back from Leeds and the eve of Mum's options conversation. Your calendar, your call, today.

17|

19|Page one of the notebook is your wedding day; the newest entry is his actual words, and you wrote slower because they cost more. You wanted to be asked, not forgiven by default — tonight, check whether the £150 leaving the account feels like being asked, and save the longer sentence for the car.
